record.paper_title: Offline Reinforcement Learning: Tutorial, Review, and Perspectives on Open Problems
record.original_question: In conservative or pessimistic value-function methods for offline reinforcement learning, how can an algorithm dynamically choose the degree of conservatism so that it avoids overestimating out-of-distribution actions without unnecessarily rejecting unfamiliar actions that may be useful for improving over the behavior policy?

evidence.quote: Indeed, excessive pessimism may be one of the bigger issues preventing better performance on current benchmarks, and an important open question is how to dynamically modulate the degree of conservatism to balance the risks of overestimation against the downside of avoiding any unfamiliar action.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an offline reinforcement learning setting in which a learner is given a fixed dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ of transitions collected by some unknown behavior policy $\pi_\beta$ in a Markov decision process $\mathcal{M} = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, r, \gamma)$, with no further interaction allowed. A standard family of algorithms estimates a value function $\hat{Q}^\pi$ together with a learned policy $\pi$ by solving an objective of the form
$$\hat{Q} \;=\; \arg\min_{Q}\; \alpha \cdot \mathcal{R}(Q, \mathcal{D}) \;+\; \mathcal{L}_{\text{TD}}(Q, \mathcal{D}),$$
where $\mathcal{L}_{\text{TD}}$ is a temporal-difference Bellman-error loss on $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{R}(Q, \mathcal{D}) \ge 0$ is a conservatism/pessimism penalty (for example, one that pushes down $Q(s,a)$ for actions $a$ that are out-of-distribution under $\pi_\beta(\cdot \mid s)$ and pushes up $Q$ on in-distribution actions). The scalar $\alpha \ge 0$ controls the strength of conservatism: large $\alpha$ prevents overestimation of unfamiliar actions but suppresses any policy improvement that requires choosing actions not well-covered by $\pi_\beta$, while small $\alpha$ permits exploitation of unfamiliar actions but risks catastrophic overestimation.

Design and analyze a procedure that, using only the offline dataset $\mathcal{D}$ (and possibly auxiliary uncertainty estimates computed from it), dynamically chooses the conservatism level — either as a global schedule $\alpha_t$ over training iterations, or as a state-action-dependent weighting $\alpha(s,a)$ on the penalty $\mathcal{R}$ — such that:

(i) the resulting Q-estimate is, with high probability, a (possibly approximate) lower bound on the true $Q^\pi$ at state-action pairs that are poorly covered by $\mathcal{D}$, thereby preventing overestimation of out-of-distribution actions; and

(ii) the learned policy $\hat{\pi}$ achieves a performance bound
$$J(\hat{\pi}) \;\ge\; J(\pi_\beta) - \varepsilon(\mathcal{D}),$$
and ideally $J(\hat{\pi}) \ge \max_\pi J(\pi) - \tilde{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{D})$ over policies whose state-action visitation is sufficiently covered by $\mathcal{D}$, without unnecessarily penalizing unfamiliar actions whose true value exceeds that of $\pi_\beta$.

Specifically: characterize, with formal guarantees, what data-driven rule for adapting $\alpha$ (or $\alpha(s,a)$) achieves an optimal tradeoff between the risk of overestimating out-of-distribution actions and the cost of rejecting beneficial unfamiliar actions, and exhibit such a rule together with finite-sample suboptimality bounds in terms of properties of $\mathcal{D}$ (e.g., concentrability, coverage, density of $\pi_\beta$).
artifact.status_search_result: Several follow-up works propose heuristic and partially analyzed approaches to dynamically modulate conservatism in offline RL — e.g., Mildly Conservative Q-Learning (MCQ), Adaptive Pessimism via Target Q-value (APTQ), and Adaptive Conservative Level in Q-Learning (ACL-QL). These provide empirical mechanisms (e.g., uncertainty- or TD-gap-based weighting) to balance overestimation against over-pessimism, but a fully satisfactory general theory with tight finite-sample guarantees for adaptively choosing the conservatism coefficient remains an active research area rather than a settled result.

status_evidence.title: Mildly Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning
status_evidence.snippet: The proper conservatism should be as mild as possible... Existing approaches, penalizing the unseen actions or regularizing with the behavior policy, are too pessimistic, which suppresses the generalization of the value function and hinders the performance improvement.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent work argues for and designs less aggressive, adaptive conservatism in offline RL.

status_evidence.title: Adaptive pessimism via target Q-value for offline reinforcement learning
status_evidence.snippet: APTQ implements adaptive pessimism by adaptively updating the loss weight for constraints according to the moving average difference between the predicted Q-value and the target Q-value.
status_evidence.claim: Adaptive schemes for tuning the pessimism weight have been proposed and partially analyzed.

status_evidence.title: ACL-QL: Adaptive Conservative Level in Q-Learning for Offline RL
status_evidence.snippet: ACL-QL is a framework that supports the fine-grained control of the conservative level in offline DRL.
status_evidence.claim: State-action-dependent adaptive conservatism levels have been explored, indicating partial progress.
